record.original_question: Is the class of linear lattices a variety? (That is, is it definable by a set of equations.)

evidence.quote: [J´ ons1953, sec. 5] Is the class of linear lattices a variety? (That is, is it definable by a set of equations.)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A lattice $L$ is called a linear lattice (or representable lattice) if it is isomorphic to a sublattice of the lattice of equivalence relations on some set $X$ in which the meet operation is intersection of equivalence relations and the join operation is the join of equivalence relations, with the additional requirement that any two elements $\alpha,\beta \in L$, viewed as equivalence relations on $X$, commute under relational composition (i.e. $\alpha\circ\beta = \beta\circ\alpha$). Equivalently, $L$ embeds into a lattice of commuting equivalence relations.

A class $\mathcal V$ of lattices is called a variety if it can be defined by a set of lattice identities (equations in the signature $\{\wedge,\vee\}$); equivalently, by Birkhoff's theorem, if it is closed under the formation of homomorphic images, sublattices, and arbitrary direct products.

Question: Is the class of all linear lattices a variety? That is, does there exist a set $\Sigma$ of lattice identities such that a lattice $L$ is linear if and only if $L$ satisfies every identity in $\Sigma$?
artifact.status_search_result: The question, originally posed by Jónsson in 1953, is widely regarded as still open. Recent surveys describe it as "the most important open question concerning linear lattices": it is known that linear lattices form a quasivariety axiomatized by an infinite set of universal Horn sentences, and Haiman (1987) showed that not every Arguesian lattice is linear, but whether the class of linear lattices is closed under homomorphic images (equivalently, equationally definable) remains unresolved.

status_evidence.title: A survey of lattice properties: modular, Arguesian, linear, and distributive
status_evidence.snippet: Constructing a linear representation of an arbitrary homomorphic image of a linear lattice would show that the class of linear lattices is a variety, answering the most important open question concerning linear lattices.
status_evidence.claim: The question whether the class of linear lattices is a variety is described in a recent survey as still open.

status_evidence.title: Proof theory for linear lattices (Haiman)
status_evidence.snippet: Linear lattices are those representable by commuting equivalence relations; they form a quasivariety.
status_evidence.claim: Linear lattices are known to form a quasivariety, but it is not known whether they form a variety.
